caption:
It boggles the mind how much BS we are fed as consumers simply because we’ve lacked tools to verify claims designed to hide a simple truth: you are being sold an undifferentiated commodity product that does nothing miraculous, as with this Medik8 sunscreen, requested by @nomadic.pack 💸

⚠️UV System & Tolerability: The UV system earns a Good verdict, falling short of the Excellent/Exceptional ratings due to likely poor solvency. It will still protect you, but we predict it’s not the best UV system on the market. It also carries a higher load of potential irritants and allergens than most sunscreens.

🤨The Actives Debunk: The brand lists 5 ingredients that “protect against environmental stressors” (whatever that means) and ‘repair the visible ageing effects of UV rays’. Here is the reality:

- Blueberry Seed Oil: Human data uses 2–6% – we estimate this formula sits at just 0.5–1.7% (likely fairy dust). Squalane is just an emollient. We count these 2 towards the Emollient & Occlusion profile, and even so, the total load is still not sufficient to provide meaningful TEWL reduction, hence the Negligible E&O verdict.

- Marrubium Vulgare Extract: No human data, just a fancy-sounding extract to justify premium pricing. 

- Plankton Extract: Human trials require a 1% photolyase liposome preparation; we estimate 0.01%–0.1% max. I wouldn’t bet on any DNA repair.

- Carnosine: Optimal concentration is ~0.5%; we estimate 0.02%–0.1% (more fairy dust).

✅On the plus side, this is a nicely hydrating product – it earns a well-deserved Advanced Hydration verdict thanks to a diverse range of humectants. However, this may also make it slightly tacky to touch.

📉The Verdict: Poor. While I’m sure it feels sensorially luxurious to use, it earns a Poor cost-effectiveness rating overall. It is simply not worth the money.
 
I will be analysing ceramide creams soon! Have one in mind you want me to analyse? Drop the name in comments 👇
